title: Elderly Activist Maricarmen, 87, Who Sparked Spain’s Eviction Protest, Dies at 87
body:
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87‑year‑old whose forced removal from a modest Madrid flat ignited a wave of street protests and a bruising political showdown, died on Wednesday while receiving care at a hospital in the capital. Her death closes a fraught chapter in Spain’s recent history, but the social and political reverberations of the eviction continue to shape debates over housing policy, elder care and the balance of power between the national government and regional authorities.  

Abascal’s eviction on March 12, 2024, was the result of a court order that allowed a private landlord to reclaim a property the octogenarian had lived in for more than half a century. The decree came after the landlord, a real‑estate firm, claimed unpaid rent and sought to redevelop the site. When police and bailiffs entered the building, a crowd of neighbors, activists and members of left‑wing parties gathered, chanting “¡No a los desahucios!” (No to evictions). The scene quickly escalated: protestors clashed with police, tear gas was deployed, and images of an elderly woman being led away under guard spread across social media, sparking nationwide outrage.  

The incident exposed deep‑seated tensions in Spain’s housing market, where soaring rents and a shortage of affordable units have left many seniors and low‑income families vulnerable. Analysts note that Madrid’s rental prices have risen by more than 30 % over the past five years, outpacing wage growth and prompting a surge in evictions. Abascal’s case became a symbol of a broader crisis, prompting the opposition Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and regional governments to demand urgent reforms, including rent caps, stronger tenant protections and a national registry of vacant homes.  

Politically, the eviction strained the coalition between Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s PSOE and the leftist Unidas Podemos, which had been navigating a fragile alliance after the 2023 elections. Unidas Podemos accused the government of tacitly supporting the landlord’s interests and called for a parliamentary inquiry. The controversy forced Sánchez to intervene, ordering a temporary suspension of evictions involving seniors and to propose a “housing emergency” package. While the measures were welcomed by many, critics argue they are insufficient and lack enforcement mechanisms, leaving the underlying market dynamics untouched.  

In the weeks following the protest, Madrid’s city council approved a moratorium on evictions for residents over 65, and the national parliament debated a bill to increase social housing construction by 20 % over the next decade. Yet opposition parties remain divided on funding sources, and the legislation has stalled amid budgetary negotiations. Meanwhile, grassroots movements have organized “housing solidarity” networks, offering legal assistance and temporary shelter to those facing displacement, echoing the solidarity that rallied around Abascal.  

María del Carmen Abascal’s passing has prompted a wave of tributes from community leaders, activists and ordinary citizens who saw her as a living embodiment of resistance against an increasingly unaffordable housing market. Memorials have been held in several neighborhoods, and a petition to rename a street in her honor has gathered thousands of signatures. While her death marks the end of a personal tragedy, the policy debates she helped catalyze are far from resolved.  

Looking ahead, Spain’s lawmakers face mounting pressure to translate the emotional response to Abascal’s eviction into concrete, enforceable reforms. The coming months will test whether the government can reconcile market liberalization with social protection, and whether the momentum generated by her story can sustain a broader movement for housing justice. The outcome will not only determine the fate of countless vulnerable tenants but also signal how democratic societies respond when the most vulnerable are thrust into the public eye.
